newsitem.title: USA: US backs IMF loan Thailand but won't give own cash.
newsitem.headline: US backs IMF loan Thailand but won't give own cash.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

The United States backs a strong IMF loan program for Thailand but does not expect to contribute its own money to a rescue package for the Southeast Asian nation, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Thursday.
"I don't expect we would be providing resources," he told Reuters in an interview.

Thailand earlier this week turned to the International Monetary Fund for financial help after its currency came under attack from investors worried about the country's excessive foreign borrowing and frail banking system.
Rubin said the United States has been working closely with both the IMF and Bangkok to help fashion an economic program to put the country's finances back into shape.

"We've been supportive of a strong IMF program that will both provide resources but also help the Thais institute the kinds of measures they need to be in a financially sound position," the Treasury chief said.

Analysts reckon that Thailand will need up to $20 billion to put its economic house in order. Japan has signalled its willingness to join in a rescue package, provided it is backed by IMF-sanctioned economic reforms.
The fallout from the Thai crisis has affected other countries in Asia, including the Philippines, which was also forced to devalue its currency and borrow from the IMF.
Rubin doubted though that Thailand's troubles posed the same sort of risks to the international financial system that Mexico's did in 1994-95.
"We have to watch and watch very carefully," he said. But, he added, "I don't think there are contagion risks anything like the magnitude you had with Mexico."
The United States led the way in putting together a $50 billion rescue package for Mexico after that country came to the brink of defaulting on its foreign loans in early 1995.
That crisis affected developing countries around the world, as frightened investors yanked money out of emerging market economies out of fear of incurring huge losses.
Rubin said international investors are more sophisticated than they were back then and have learned to better distinguish one emerging market economy from the other.
The international community, including the IMF, is also better prepared, he added.
The IMF used fast-track regulations drawn up after the Mexico crisis to approve a $1.1 billion loan for the Philippines earlier this month.
Rubin praised Manila for moving quickly to deal with the financial fallout from Thailand's currency crisis. "I thought they handled themselves extremely well," he said.
Speaking to an investment conference in New York, Rubin's deputy, Lawrence Summers, cautioned against overestimating the problems facing the one high-flying economies of Asia.
That was the message from the World Bank as well.
Javad Khalilzadeh-Shirazi, acting vice president for the bank's East Asia and Pacific region, said in a statement the economies in the region remained in good shape.
"Many have high savings rates, low or non-existent fiscal deficits and a strong export base," he said.

The statement said that the World Bank backed Thailand's decision to put together a program of IMF-backed reforms and that the lending agency was prepared "to support the government in its structural reform efforts."
